title: Research Bite #3: A Marked Improvement?
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #3 covers “A Marked Improvement? A Review of the Evidence on Written Marking,” an Education Endowment Foundation and Oxford University review of what the research base actually says about marking practices. The review's headline finding is a warning about the evidence itself: high-quality research on written marking is thin, and what does exist is often small-scale or drawn from higher education and English-as-a-foreign-language settings rather than UK primary and secondary classrooms. Even so, several threads recur across the studies the authors do trust: marking should distinguish careless mistakes (simply flagged as wrong) from misunderstanding-driven errors (addressed with hints or guiding questions), awarding a grade alongside every piece of work can crowd out attention to formative comments, and marking is only useful if pupils are given dedicated time to actually read and act on it. The review's most quoted line reframes the whole workload conversation: schools should mark less, but mark better. Barton's classroom implication is a permission slip as much as a finding — the volume of red ink a teacher produces is not the metric that matters; whether pupils use it is.
points: The review's most striking finding may be about the evidence base itself: high-quality, classroom-based research on written marking is scarce, so many common marking policies rest on thinner evidence than teachers might assume.

The careless-mistake vs. misunderstanding distinction gives teachers a concrete triage rule: flag careless errors as simply wrong, but address misunderstanding-driven errors with hints or questions that lead pupils to the underlying principle.
Grading every piece of work risks undercutting the marking itself — when pupils fixate on the grade, they are less likely to engage with the formative comments sitting next to it.
Marking only pays off if class time is deliberately set aside for pupils to read and respond to it — feedback pupils never revisit cannot improve their work.

The review's mantra — “mark less, but mark better” — reframes marking workload debates around impact rather than volume, and is echoed by the 2016 Independent Teacher Workload Review Group's finding that written feedback had become disproportionately valued by quantity over quality.
quotes: This review of marking practices, commissioned by the Education Endowment Foundation (EEF), examines the evidence for a variety of marking approaches. The review notes a dearth of high-quality research in this area, particularly in primary and secondary school settings.
The quality of existing evidence focused specifically on written marking is low. Few large-scale, robust studies have examined marking practices.

Teachers should differentiate between careless mistakes and errors resulting from misunderstanding. Errors resulting from misunderstanding may be best addressed by providing hints or questions that lead pupils to underlying principles.
Awarding grades for every piece of work may reduce the impact of marking, particularly if pupils become preoccupied with grades at the expense of considering teachers’ formative comments.
Pupils are unlikely to benefit from marking unless some time is set aside to enable pupils to consider and respond to marking.
A mantra might be that schools should mark less in terms of the number of pieces of work marked, but mark better.

Additionally, a 2016 report from the Independent Teacher Workload Review Group suggested that providing written feedback on pupils’ work has become disproportionately valued by schools, and the quantity of feedback has too often become confused with quality.
